ruminate about how to get even with assailant

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
Nothing good can happen to me anymore
I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

vignette: Kamran still remembers the day the earthquake hit his hometown in Iran like it was yesterday. He was just a teenager then, and the sound of crumbling buildings and screams still echoes in his mind. His family had been lucky to escape with their lives, but the experience left an indelible mark on Kamran's psyche. As he grew older, Kamran became increasingly withdrawn and isolated. He couldn't shake off the feeling that nothing good could happen to him anymore (No Good Ahead). Every creak of the floor or sudden movement nearby made him jump, as if he was always waiting for another disaster to strike (Startle to Movement). He began to identify escape routes wherever he went, a habit that brought him some semblance of comfort in unfamiliar environments (Escape Route Planning). Kamran's memories of the earthquake were fragmented and disordered, like pieces of a puzzle he couldn't quite fit together (Confused Sequence). When they came flooding back, they felt completely real - he could smell the dust, feel the ground shaking beneath his feet, and hear the deafening roar of collapsing buildings (Full Sensory Reliving). The auditory recall was particularly distressing; he would often hear the screams of those trapped under the rubble, or the sound of his own heartbeat pounding in his ears. As a software engineer, Kamran's work required him to focus on logical problems, but his mind kept wandering back to that fateful day. He began to ruminate about how he could have done things differently (Rumination: Revenge), replaying scenarios where he saved more people or escaped unscathed. These thoughts led him down a rabbit hole of self-blame and recrimination, making him wonder if someone else would not have gotten into this situation in the first place (Self-Comparison). Kamran tried to force himself to think only positive thoughts (Positive Reframing), but it was like trying to hold back a tide. The more he pushed away the negative emotions, the stronger they seemed to come back. He started avoiding hospitals and medical cues, fearful of being reminded of his own mortality or vulnerability (Avoid Medical Cues). His wife grew concerned about his increasing withdrawal from social interactions, but Kamran couldn't explain why the sound of someone touching him unexpectedly made him react with alarm (Startle to Touch). As time went on, Kamran's maladaptive strategies only seemed to exacerbate his symptoms. The more he tried to escape or distract himself, the more his memories and negative appraisals seemed to resurface (Memory -> Maladaptive Strategies). His startle response grew stronger, making him feel like he was constantly walking on eggshells (Threat -> Memory). Kamran's sense of self-worth continued to erode; he felt lost and miserable, unable to find happiness in the things that once brought him joy (Lost Happiness). It wasn't until his wife sat him down for a heart-to-heart talk that Kamran realized he needed help. She pointed out how his constant hypervigilance was affecting their relationship and daily life. For the first time, Kamran saw how his symptoms were interconnected - how his negative appraisals fed into his threat perception, which in turn fueled his maladaptive strategies (Negative Appraisals -> Threat -> Maladaptive Strategies). He knew he couldn't keep living like this; it was time to face his demons head-on. With a deep breath, Kamran agreed to seek professional help, hoping to break the cycle of fear and self-blame that had held him captive for so long.
